q: Which piece of apparatus is best for measuring exactly 25.0 cm³ of aqueous sodium hydroxide into a conical flask?
options: a volumetric pipette
a 100 cm³ measuring cylinder
a gas syringe
a 250 cm³ beaker
explain: A volumetric pipette delivers one fixed volume very accurately. A measuring cylinder is less accurate, a gas syringe measures gases and a beaker is only roughly graduated.

q: Which apparatus is used to measure the volume of a gas given off during a reaction?
options: a volumetric pipette
a balance
a gas syringe
a thermometer
explain: A gas syringe collects the gas and the plunger moves out so the volume can be read from the scale. The other items measure liquid volume, mass or temperature.

q: Which row correctly pairs the apparatus with the quantity it measures?
options: stop-watch | temperature
balance | mass
burette | mass
thermometer | time
explain: A balance measures mass. A stop-watch measures time, a burette measures volume of liquid and a thermometer measures temperature.

q: Sugar is stirred into water until all of it dissolves. Which row correctly names the solute and the solvent?
options: water | sugar
sugar solution | sugar
sugar | sugar solution
sugar | water
explain: The solute is the substance that dissolves (sugar) and the solvent is the substance it dissolves in (water). The mixture of the two is the solution.

q: Which statement describes a saturated solution?
options: It contains more solute than solvent.
It contains no dissolved solute at all.
It contains the maximum concentration of solute that can dissolve in the solvent at a given temperature.
It contains the maximum mass of solute that can dissolve at any temperature.
explain: A saturated solution holds as much dissolved solute as it can at a stated temperature, so any extra solute stays undissolved. The amount that can dissolve changes with temperature.

q: A mixture of chalk powder and water is poured through filter paper. Which statement is correct?
options: The chalk is the residue and the water is the filtrate.
The chalk is the filtrate and the water is the residue.
The chalk and the water are both the filtrate.
The water is the residue and the chalk is the solvent.
explain: The solid that stays on the filter paper is the residue; the liquid that passes through is the filtrate.

q: Which of these is a solution?
options: sand stirred into water
oil shaken with water
chalk powder stirred into water
salt dissolved in water
explain: A solution is a solute completely dissolved in a solvent. Sand, oil and chalk do not dissolve in water, so they do not form solutions.

q: A student adds acid to an alkali in a titration. What is one advantage of using a burette rather than a measuring cylinder to add the acid?
options: It can measure the volume of a gas as well.
The volume added can be controlled drop by drop and read more precisely.
It measures the mass of acid added.
It is quicker to fill and read.
explain: A burette has a tap and a fine scale so small volumes can be added slowly and read accurately, which is needed to find an end-point.

q: Which apparatus would be used to measure the mass of a solid to the nearest 0.01 g?
options: a balance
a measuring cylinder
a thermometer
a stop-watch
explain: A balance measures mass. A measuring cylinder measures volume, a thermometer measures temperature and a stop-watch measures time.

q: Which gas cannot be collected over water because it is very soluble in water?
options: hydrogen
oxygen
nitrogen
ammonia
explain: Ammonia dissolves very readily in water, so collecting it over water would lose the gas. Hydrogen, oxygen and nitrogen are only slightly soluble.

q: A student follows the rate of a reaction that produces a gas. Which pair of apparatus is most suitable?
options: a volumetric pipette and a balance
a gas syringe and a stop-watch
a thermometer and a burette
a measuring cylinder and a thermometer
explain: The volume of gas must be measured at regular times, so a gas syringe and a stop-watch are needed. The other pairs cannot measure gas volume against time.

q: Zinc reacts with excess dilute acid to give hydrogen gas. Why is measuring the loss in mass of the flask a poor way to follow this reaction?
options: Hydrogen dissolves in the acid so no mass is lost.
A balance cannot be used with an acid.
The mass of hydrogen lost is so small that it is difficult to measure accurately.
Hydrogen is denser than air so it stays in the flask.
explain: Hydrogen has a very low relative molecular mass, so the mass lost is tiny compared with the sensitivity of a typical balance.

q: Extra solid is added to a saturated solution at constant temperature and stirred. What happens?
options: The extra solid dissolves and the solution stays saturated.
The extra solid stays undissolved because the maximum concentration has already been reached.
The extra solid dissolves and the solution becomes unsaturated.
The solid reacts with the solvent.
explain: A saturated solution cannot dissolve more solute at that temperature, so the added solid remains as a residue at the bottom.

q: In an experiment to measure a temperature change, a student uses a polystyrene cup instead of a glass beaker. What is the advantage?
options: Polystyrene is a better insulator so less heat is lost to the surroundings.
Polystyrene conducts heat better so the temperature changes faster.
Polystyrene reacts with the solution so the change is bigger.
Polystyrene is transparent so the solution can be seen.
explain: Polystyrene is a poor conductor of heat, so less energy escapes and the measured temperature change is closer to the true value.

q: Which description of an acid–base titration is correct?
options: A measuring cylinder puts exactly 25.0 cm³ of acid into a burette and alkali is added from a conical flask.
Indicator is placed in the burette and acid is poured into the conical flask all at once.
A volumetric pipette puts a fixed volume of alkali into a conical flask, indicator is added and acid is run in from a burette until the colour changes.
Alkali is run from a burette into a volumetric pipette until the indicator changes colour.
explain: The pipette measures one accurate volume into the flask. The burette adds the other solution gradually until the indicator shows the end-point.

q: Dilute hydrochloric acid is added slowly to aqueous sodium hydroxide containing methyl orange. What colour change shows the end-point?
options: red to yellow
yellow to blue
colourless to pink
yellow to orange
explain: Methyl orange is yellow in alkali and red in acid, so the end-point is the first permanent change from yellow to orange when acid is added to alkali.

q: Dilute acid is added to aqueous sodium hydroxide containing thymolphthalein. What colour change shows the end-point?
options: colourless to blue
blue to colourless
red to yellow
pink to colourless
explain: Thymolphthalein is blue in alkali and colourless in acid, so adding acid to alkali causes a change from blue to colourless.

q: What is the purpose of the indicator in a titration?
options: to speed up the neutralisation reaction
to make the mixture neutral
to measure the volume of acid added
to show the point at which the acid and alkali have exactly reacted
explain: An indicator changes colour at the end-point, showing when exactly enough acid has been added to neutralise the alkali.

q: Why is a burette rinsed with a little of the acid it is going to contain before it is filled?
options: Acid cleans the tap so it can be turned more easily.
Acid in the burette speeds up the reaction in the flask.
Water left in the burette would dilute the acid and make the titre wrong.
Rinsing with acid makes the end-point easier to see.
explain: Any water left in the burette would lower the concentration of the acid, so the volume needed would not match the stated concentration.

q: 25.0 cm³ of aqueous sodium hydroxide is neutralised by 20.0 cm³ of 0.100 mol/dm³ hydrochloric acid. What is the concentration of the sodium hydroxide?
options: 0.0800 mol/dm³
0.125 mol/dm³
0.100 mol/dm³
0.0400 mol/dm³
explain: Moles HCl = 0.0200 × 0.100 = 0.00200 mol. HCl and NaOH react 1 : 1, so concentration of NaOH = 0.00200 ÷ 0.0250 = 0.0800 mol/dm³.

q: 25.0 cm³ of 0.200 mol/dm³ sulfuric acid is neutralised by 20.0 cm³ of aqueous sodium hydroxide: H₂SO₄ + 2NaOH → Na₂SO₄ + 2H₂O. What is the concentration of the sodium hydroxide?
options: 0.250 mol/dm³
0.200 mol/dm³
0.500 mol/dm³
1.00 mol/dm³
explain: Moles H₂SO₄ = 0.0250 × 0.200 = 0.00500 mol. Moles NaOH = 2 × 0.00500 = 0.0100 mol. Concentration = 0.0100 ÷ 0.0200 = 0.500 mol/dm³.

q: Why is a titration repeated until two results agree closely?
options: so that the results are reliable and a mean titre can be calculated
so that all the acid is used up
to make the indicator change colour faster
to increase the concentration of the alkali
explain: Titres that agree closely (concordant results) show that the measurements are reliable, so they can be averaged to give an accurate value.

q: Which row correctly describes the use of the apparatus in a titration?
options: volumetric pipette | adds a variable volume of solution drop by drop
burette | adds a variable volume of solution drop by drop
conical flask | measures an exact volume of solution
burette | measures exactly 25.0 cm³ each time
explain: The burette delivers any volume needed and can be controlled drop by drop. The pipette delivers one fixed volume and the conical flask only holds the mixture.

q: A student titrates an acid with an alkali to prepare pure crystals of a salt. Why is the titration repeated without indicator using the same volumes?
options: The indicator would react with the acid to form a gas.
The reaction only works if no indicator is present.
The indicator would make the solution more acidic.
The indicator would contaminate the salt crystals.
explain: The indicator is needed only to find the volumes that neutralise each other. Repeating without it gives a salt solution that is not contaminated by the dye.

q: Which row gives the correct colours of the indicator in acid and in alkali?
options: methyl orange | yellow | red
methyl orange | red | yellow
thymolphthalein | blue | colourless
litmus | blue | red
explain: Methyl orange is red in acid and yellow in alkali. Thymolphthalein is colourless in acid and blue in alkali, and litmus is red in acid and blue in alkali.

q: In a titration the burette reading at the start is 3.10 cm³ and at the end-point is 23.30 cm³. What is the volume of acid added?
explain: The volume added is the final reading minus the initial reading: 23.30 − 3.10 = 20.20 cm³.

q: In paper chromatography the starting line is drawn in pencil rather than ink. Why?
options: Pencil does not dissolve in the solvent, so it will not move up the paper.
Pencil is a better solvent than ink.
Ink would react with the paper.
Pencil lines make the spots move faster.
explain: Ink contains dyes that would dissolve and run with the solvent. Pencil (graphite) is insoluble, so the line stays put and does not interfere.

q: A student places the spot of ink below the level of the solvent in the beaker. What is the most likely result?
options: The substances separate more clearly.
The solvent runs faster up the paper.
The coloured substances dissolve into the solvent and no chromatogram forms.
The ink spot becomes insoluble.
explain: The solvent level must be below the starting line so that the spot is carried up the paper rather than washed away into the solvent.

q: What does a single spot on a chromatogram suggest about a coloured substance?
options: It is definitely a mixture.
It must be an element.
It could be pure because it has not separated into more than one substance.
It is insoluble in the solvent.
explain: A pure substance gives one spot, but one spot is only evidence of purity: it is also useful to run it in more than one solvent.

q: A chromatogram of an unknown dye X shows two spots. Pure dyes A, B and C each give one spot. The spots from X match the heights of the spots from A and C. What does this show?
options: X is a pure substance.
X is a mixture of three of the dyes.
X contains only B.
X is a mixture of dye A and dye C.
explain: Spots that travel the same distance in the same solvent are the same substance. X has two spots that match A and C, so it is a mixture of those two.
